title: Can the firm prove a change is safe before it spreads?
mainJudgement: Can the firm prove a change is safe before it spreads?

deepDive.title: It was never about the model. It’s about the harness.
deepDive.dek: What the FCA and FSB's latest warnings mean for remediation capacity, control design and correlated cyber disruption.

committeeQuestion.question: Before an AI-assisted, supplier-led or regulatory change moves further, what proves that it is understood, authorised and safe to operate?
committeeQuestion.why: This week's evidence moves from agent-assisted code change and critical providers to complaint intelligence, exploited vulnerabilities and e-invoicing platforms. In each case, speed without a clear evidence trail is the avoidable risk.
committeeQuestion.evidence: The change record, affected-service and data map, named decision-maker, test or parity result, supplier or control dependency, approved exception, recovery route and dated closure evidence.

committeeQuestions.question: Which critical service relies on a supplier or platform whose failure would leave us unable to contain, recover or explain a decision?
committeeQuestions.why: The BIS consultation brings cyber resilience and third-party dependence into the same operating conversation. AWS's investigation guidance shows the incident record needed when that dependency fails.
committeeQuestions.evidence: The service map, critical suppliers, intervention and escalation authority, tested fallback, incident timeline, recovery decision record and evidence that the service was safe to resume.

committeeQuestions.question: Can we turn a customer report, vulnerability alert or data-control exception into an owned action before it becomes an external finding?
committeeQuestions.why: ASIC's misconduct data and CISA's exploited-vulnerability update both show that available signals only matter when they reach a person with authority to investigate and act.
committeeQuestions.evidence: The intake route, triage criteria, named owner, decision log, remediation or compensating control, customer or control impact, independent retest and closed-loop reporting.

judgement.observation: Mistral’s agent-led code-modernisation case begins with a parity harness. BIS is consulting on FMI cyber resilience and third-party dependence. ASIC shows misconduct reporting feeding surveillance; CISA has added three exploited flaws; CNIL has set out the operating roles around live e-invoicing.
judgement.executiveJudgement: These are different changes, but none is safely managed by a policy alone. The control has to keep pace with the change: what is affected, who can decide, what shows the outcome is right, and how the firm will contain or reverse it if it is not.
judgement.implication: Choose one live change. Bring the owner, service and data map, supplier or control dependency, test result, intervention route, exception record and closure evidence into the next leadership conversation.

topSignals.title: AI-assisted legacy-code change needs a parity harness before it needs scale
topSignals.label: AI change control
topSignals.why: Agentic implementation needs a testable baseline and human approval gates before it changes production code at scale.

topSignals.title: BIS puts critical third-party dependence inside the cyber-resilience test
topSignals.label: Critical dependency
topSignals.why: The consultation connects supplier reliance, intervention rights and recovery evidence for financial market infrastructures.

topSignals.title: ASIC's misconduct data turns reporting channels into a control-intelligence test
topSignals.label: Intelligence to action
topSignals.why: Reports must reach a team that can triage, investigate, act and show the result rather than remain a passive volume metric.

topSignals.title: Three new exploited flaws test whether the patch queue maps to the estate
topSignals.label: Emergency closure
